title: What Christ suffered was not defilement
source_text: Ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ ποιεῖ ἢ πάσχει αἴσχιστα ὁ θεὸς οὐδὲ τῷ κακῷ διακονεῖται, ὡς οἴεται Κέλσος· οὐδὲ γὰρ προείρηταί τι τῶν τοιούτων. κἂν λέγῃ αὐτὸς προειρῆσθαι τὸν θεὸν τῷ κακῷ διακονεῖσθαι ἢ ποιεῖν ἢ πάσχειν αἴσχιστα, ἔμελλε παραθέσθαι τὰς ἀπὸ τῶν προφητῶν εἰς τοῦτο λέξεις καὶ μὴ μάτην μολύνειν ἐθέλειν τοὺς ἀκούοντας αὐτοῦ. ἃ μὲν οὖν πείσεται Χριστὸς προεῖπον οἱ προφῆται, καὶ τὴν αἰτίαν τιθέντες τοῦ, δι᾿ ὃ πείσεται· καὶ ὁ θεὸς ἠπίστατο ἅπερ ὁ Χριστὸς αὐτοῦ πείσεται. πόθεν δ᾿ ὅτι καὶ μιαρώτατα καὶ ἀκαθαρτότατα ταῦτ᾿ ἦν, ὥς φησιν ὁ Κέλσος; ἀλλὰ δόξει διδάσκειν, πῶς μιαρώτατα καὶ ἀκαθαρτότατ᾿ ἄττα ἦν ἃ καὶ ὑπέμεινεν, ἐπεί φησι· τί γὰρ ἄλλο ἦν θεῷ τὸ προβάτων σάρκας ἐσθίειν καὶ χολὴν ἣ ὄξος πίνειν πλὴν σκατοφαγεῖν; θεὸς δὲ καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς προβάτων σάρκας οὐκ ησθιεν. ἵνα γὰρ καὶ δόξῃ ὅτι ἤσθιεν, ὡς σῶμα φορῶν ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἤσθιεν. ἀλλὰ καὶ περὶ τῆς χολῆς καὶ τοῦ ὄξους, προφητευθέντων ἐν τῷ „ἔδωκαν εἰς τὸ βρῶμά μου χολὴν, καὶ εἰς τὴν δίψαν μου ἐπότισάν με ὄξος,“ ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω προειρηκότες ἀναγκαζόμεθα ὑπὸ τοῦ Κέλσου παλιλλογεῖν. ἀεὶ γὰρ οἱ τῷ τῆς ἀληθείας ἐπιβουλεύοντες λόγῳ χολὴν τὴν ἀπὸ τῆς ἑαυτῶν κακίας καὶ ὄξος τὸ ἀπὸ τῆς ἰδίας ἐπὶ τὰ φαῦλα τροπῆς προσάγουσι τῷ Χριστῷ τοῦ θεοῦ, ὃς „γευσάμενος οὐ θέλει πιεῖν.“
pass_a_gloss: But neither does God do (ποιέω) or suffer (πάσχω) most shameful things (αἴσχιστος), nor serve (διακονέομαι) evil (τὸ κακόν), as Celsus thinks (οἴομαι); for nothing of such things has been foretold (προλέγω). And if he says himself it was foretold that God serves evil or does or suffers most shameful things, he was bound (μέλλω) to quote (παρατίθημι) the words (λέξεις) from the prophets to this point, and not in vain (μάτην) to wish to pollute (μολύνω) those hearing him. What Christ will suffer the prophets foretold, also setting down the cause (αἰτία) on account of which he will suffer; and God knew (ἐπίσταμαι) what his Christ will suffer. But whence that these things were most polluted (μιαρώτατος) and most unclean (ἀκαθαρτότατος), as Celsus says? But he will seem to teach how the things he endured (ὑπομένω) were most polluted and most unclean, since he says: 'for what else was it for God to eat (ἐσθίω) flesh (σάρξ) of sheep (πρόβατον) and drink gall (χολή) or vinegar (ὄξος) except to eat dung (σκατοφαγέω)?' But God according to us did not eat sheep's flesh. For even if it should seem (δοκέω) that he ate, Jesus ate as bearing (φορέω) a body (σῶμα). But concerning the gall and vinegar, prophesied in 'they gave into my food (βρῶμα) gall, and for my thirst (δίψα) they gave me vinegar to drink (ποτίζω)', having spoken before in the earlier parts (ἀνωτέρω) we are compelled (ἀναγκάζω) by Celsus to repeat (παλιλλογέω). For always those plotting against (ἐπιβουλεύω) the word (λόγος) of truth bring (προσάγω) to the Christ of God the gall from their own wickedness (κακία) and the vinegar from their own turning (τροπή) toward base things (τὰ φαῦλα), he who 'having tasted (γεύομαι) will not drink'.
pass_b_english: But God neither does nor suffers the most shameful things, nor does he serve evil, as Celsus supposes; for nothing of the kind was foretold. And if he himself says that it was foretold that God would serve evil, or do or suffer the most shameful things, he ought to have quoted the prophets’ words to that effect, instead of wishing to defile his hearers to no purpose.

What Christ would suffer, the prophets did foretell, and they also set down the reason why he would suffer; and God knew what his Christ would suffer. But on what grounds were these things most foul and most unclean, as Celsus says? He will seem, though, to be showing how the things Christ endured were most foul and most unclean, since he says: “For what else was it for God to eat the flesh of sheep and to drink gall or vinegar, but to eat dung?”

But God, on our teaching, did not eat the flesh of sheep. For even supposing he did eat, it was as one who bore a body that Jesus ate. As for the gall and the vinegar, which were prophesied in the words, “They gave gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Psalm 69:21), we have spoken of them earlier, and Celsus forces us to say it again. For those who plot against the word of truth always bring to the Christ of God the gall that comes from their own wickedness and the vinegar that comes from their own turning toward what is base; and he, “when he has tasted it, will not drink” (Matthew 27:34).

choices.choice: Psalm 68:22 LXX = Psalm 69:21 English. Matthew 27:34: Origen’s form (ou thelei piein, present) differs slightly from the Gospel text (ouk ethelen piein); the present tense is kept (‘will not drink’) because Origen applies it to what Christ always does. The source prints χολὴν ἣ ὄξος in Celsus’s words; read ἢ (‘or’). θεῷ in Celsus’s mouth is anarthrous; rendered ‘God’ because he mocks the Christian claim that Jesus is God, and Origen answers with θεὸς καθ’ ἡμᾶς. ἵνα γὰρ καὶ δόξῃ ὅτι ἤσθιεν read as concessive (‘even supposing he did eat’). ‘Spoken of them earlier’ points back to an earlier book of Against Celsus (likely 2.37); not cited inline since unverified. σκατοφαγεῖν rendered plainly as ‘eat dung’. ‘The flesh of sheep’ may glance at the Passover lamb; not stated in the Greek, so no citation. The unnamed subject of ὑπέμεινεν is made explicit as ‘Christ’.
'and not wish to defile' smoothed to 'instead of wishing to defile' (μὴ ... ἐθέλειν)
πόθεν: 'where does it come from that' (calque) -> 'on what grounds were these things'
δόξει διδάσκειν: 'to be teaching' -> 'to be showing'
'even if it be granted that he ate' (archaic subjunctive) -> 'even supposing he did eat'
restored the omitted γάρ ('For those who plot...')
οὐ θέλει present kept: 'would not drink' -> 'will not drink'
Scripture checked: Psalm 68:22 LXX = 69:21 English (wording matches); Matthew 27:34 (γευσάμενος οὐκ ἤθελεν πιεῖν) confirmed
Celsus's quoted words kept in double quotation marks; Origen's reply kept outside them
